lead: A rigid body may carry many forces at many points. The same net push and the same net turning effect can be produced by one force and one couple. This chapter reduces any force system to a resultant R at a chosen point O plus a moment M_O about O. It then tests when the pair collapses to a single force. The idea is used to find reactions on beams, machines and plates without solving every force separately, and to spot a leftover pure couple.

blocks.text: Two force systems are equivalent when they give the same sum of forces and the same sum of moments about one point. If both match at one point O, they match at every point of a rigid body. The reduced pair is R and M_O. R is the resultant force vector in N. M_O is the resultant moment vector about O in N·m. For each force F_i acting at point r_i, add F_i to R and add r_i × F_i to M_O. The point O is only a bookkeeping point; it may lie outside the body. This reduction is the base for reactions and for checking whether a complicated loading can be replaced by one force.
R = ΣF,    M_O = Σ M_O = Σ (r × F)
blocks.where: R is the resultant force vector in N; F is each force vector in N; M_O is the resultant moment vector about O in N·m; r is the position vector from O to the point of application in m; × is the vector cross product; Σ means sum over all forces.

blocks.text: Use the same point O for every force when you compare two systems. Changing O changes M_O, but not R. The equivalence test must use one chosen point.

When R ≠ 0, split M_O into a part along R and a part perpendicular to R. Shift the force by a perpendicular distance to cancel the perpendicular part. A force plus a parallel couple remains: a wrench. If R·M_O = 0, the parallel part is zero, so only a single force is left. Its perpendicular offset from O is d = |M_O| / |R|. The vector relation is r × R = M_O. A nonzero dot product means M_O has a component along R; a single force cannot create that, because r × R is always perpendicular to R.

items: R·M_O = 0 and R ≠ 0: one force of magnitude R at perpendicular distance d = |M_O| / |R| from O.
R = 0 and M_O ≠ 0: a pure couple; no single force can replace it.
R parallel to M_O: a wrench, meaning a force with a couple along its own line.
R = 0 and M_O = 0: equilibrium under the reduced system; see equilibrium of rigid bodies.

blocks.where: d is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action in m; |M_O| is the magnitude of the moment about O in N·m; |R| is the magnitude of the resultant force in N.

blocks.text: For forces in the xy plane, resolve every force into x and y components. Sum the components to get R_x and R_y. Sum moments about O with one sign convention. Take anticlockwise positive. Then use Varignon's theorem to place the resultant line.
R_x = ΣF_x,   R_y = ΣF_y,   |R| = √(R_x² + R_y²),   θ = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x)
blocks.where: R_x and R_y are resultant components in N; F_x and F_y are force components in N; |R| is the resultant magnitude in N; θ is the angle from the +x axis.
M_O is the moment about O in N·m, anticlockwise positive; x, y are the coordinates of the point of application in m; F_x, F_y are the force components in N.

items: Choose O and write the sign convention for moments.
Resolve each force into x and y components.
Add components to get R_x and R_y, then |R| and θ.
Add moments about O to get M_O.
Locate the line of action: if R_y ≠ 0, the x-intercept is x = M_O / R_y at y = 0; if R_y = 0, the line is y = −M_O / R_x.

blocks.text: A distributed load is handled by the same reduction. Its resultant equals the area under the load diagram and acts at the centroid of that area. Centroids of areas are covered in Unit 4, Centroids and Moments of Inertia.

figure.caption: A general force system becomes R at O plus M_O; the test R·M_O = 0 decides whether a single shifted force replaces the pair.

spec.title: Reduction at O
spec.aria: A general force system is reduced to a resultant R and a moment M about a point O; if R dot M is zero the pair collapses to a single force shifted by d, otherwise a wrench or a couple remains.

examples.question: Three coplanar forces act on a plate: F₁ = 10 N along +y at A(0, 0), F₂ = 20 N along +x at B(0, 2) m, and F₃ = 15 N along −y at C(4, 0) m. Find the resultant and where its line of action cuts the x-axis.
steps: Take +x right, +y up, and anticlockwise moment positive about O(0, 0).
Write the forces: F₁ = 10j N at (0, 0); F₂ = 20i N at (0, 2) m; F₃ = −15j N at (4, 0) m.
Direction: tan θ = |R_y| / R_x = 5 / 20 = 0.25, so θ = 14.0° below the +x axis.
Moment of F₂ about O: 0·0 − 2·20 = −40 N·m, clockwise.
Moment of F₃ about O: 4·(−15) − 0·0 = −60 N·m, clockwise.
On the x-axis y = 0. The moment of R there is xR_y = x(−5). Set x(−5) = −100, so x = 20 m.
examples.answer: The resultant is 20.6 N at 14.0° below the +x axis, cutting the x-axis at 20 m from O and turning the plate clockwise.
examples.check:
import math
Rx = 20.0
Ry = -5.0
MO = -100.0
R = math.hypot(Rx, Ry)
ang = math.degrees(math.atan2(-Ry, Rx))
x = MO / Ry
print(round(R, 1))
print(round(ang, 1))
print(round(MO, 1))
print(round(x, 1))

traps: Do not sum moments about different points for different forces; choose O once and keep it.
R = 0 does not mean equilibrium when M_O ≠ 0; a pure couple is left over.
Keep one sign convention. In the xy plane M_O = Σ(xF_y − yF_x) is anticlockwise positive, not yF_x − xF_y.
For a single-force offset, use d = |M_O| / |R| with M_O about the same O; do not mix a moment about another point.
Convert cm or mm to m before computing moments, so force times distance gives N·m.

quiz.a: Two force systems are equivalent when they produce the same sum of forces and the same sum of moments about one point, and therefore about every point of a rigid body.

quiz.q: Why does matching ΣF and ΣM about one point imply matching about every point?
quiz.a: The difference of the two systems has zero force and zero moment about O. A zero-force system has the same moment about every point, so the difference also has zero moment about every point.

quiz.q: A 30 N force acts at (2, 0) m along +y. A 40 N force acts at (0, 3) m along +x. Find R and M_O about O.
R = 5i N and M_O = 20k N·m about O. Can the system become a single force? Find its offset.
quiz.a: R·M_O = 0, so yes. d = |M_O| / |R| = 20 / 5 = 4 m. The line is y = −4 m, because r × R = (x i + y j) × 5i = −5y k must equal 20k.

quiz.q: A system reduces to R = 0 and M_O = 6 N·m. What is it, and is it equilibrium?
quiz.a: It is a pure couple of 6 N·m. It is not equilibrium, because a couple remains even though the force sum is zero.

quiz.q: A system reduces to R = 10i N and M_O = 30i N·m. What reduction remains? Why not a single force?
quiz.a: A wrench: a 10 N force along +x plus a 30 N·m couple parallel to it. R·M_O = 300 ≠ 0, so the moment has a component along R. A single force cannot produce a moment along its own line, because r × R is perpendicular to R.

quiz.q: Write the moment formula for a coplanar force about O.
quiz.a: M_O = xF_y − yF_x, with x and y in m, F_x and F_y in N, and M_O in N·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. Force reduction becomes screw theory in robotics, where every motion and every load is written as a twist or a wrench. Multibody dynamics software uses the same reduction at every joint to build equations of motion. Finite element codes reduce element loads to nodal forces and moments. Search next for wrench, screw theory and equivalent force systems in spatial mechanics.
